description: We are beginner/intermediate developers and are interested in edtech and gamified learning!
summary:
Painted Outpost is a browser game for ages 7 to 12. You are an astronaut keeping a small base running at Gale Crater on Mars, on real dates, under the real sky. The ground under your feet is NASA's one-metre map of Gale Crater. The Sun, Earth, the moons and 925 stars sit where they really were at that minute. One chapter is May 20, 2024, when a real solar storm hit Mars: you get a warning, run for shelter, and then see your radiation dose beside what the Curiosity rover measured.
It trains the way astronauts train: by doing. You brush dust off solar panels, trace a cut power line and join its wires, choose which machine gets power, and pay for every job in suit time. Everything on screen is labelled real or made up, with its source, so children learn what we know about Mars and how we know it.
details:
Painted Outpost is a third-person game that runs in a web browser, with nothing to install. The player walks an astronaut round a small base at Gale Crater on Mars and keeps three things flowing: power, water and air. The whole world is drawn as an oil painting, and the paint is the display. A machine with power keeps its colour. A cut line goes grey past the break, so a child finds the fault by following the colour. A paint palette in the corner shows power, water and air as three blobs that grow and shrink.

There are six chapters, each set on real dates. The first is a lesson that waits for the player to do each thing, with an arrow to follow. The second is May 20, 2024, when a real solar storm hit Mars: a warning ring counts down, the player runs for shelter, and afterwards their dose is set beside the 8,100 micrograys the Curiosity rover measured. The third is November 2023, when Mars went behind the Sun and NASA stopped sending commands, so three things break and nobody can help. In the fourth, a dusty day leaves too little power for everything and the player chooses what stays on. In the fifth, the player makes oxygen from Mars air for the trip home without leaving the base dark at night. The last shows the sky over Gale Crater at this moment, from a table saved ahead of time.

Jobs are done by hand. The player rubs the dust off the solar panels, drags each wire of a cut line to its twin, and picks icy soil off a belt while leaving the rocks. Quick, careful work costs less suit time and mistakes cost more, so every job is a trade against the hours left in the suit. Each day ends with up to three stars: the base still runs, nothing is left broken, and nothing ran down.

The real data does work in the game. The ground is the HiRISE one-metre elevation model of Gale Crater, with the 25 centimetre orbital image for its brightness. The Sun, Earth, Phobos and Deimos are placed from NASA JPL Horizons tables worked out for the base's exact spot, so the real Sun is what charges the panels. The night sky is painted from 925 real stars, turned with the standard model of how Mars spins; we checked that against Horizons and it agrees to within 0.008 degrees. A telescope at the base aims the game's own camera at that sky, and clicking a star swings the view to it and gives its name and distance. Mars time of day follows NASA's Mars24 method. A strip on screen always shows three real numbers: the time on Mars, the Sun's height, and how many minutes a radio call takes to reach Earth. Fact cards appear when the player meets the real thing, such as the Space Station reusing 98 of every 100 drops of its water, MOXIE making oxygen from Mars air, and dust cutting the InSight lander's power.

Every number shown is marked Real, Real and worked out, From the game, or Made up. The crew and their base are made up, and the game says so. A Sources page in the base computer lists every data file and where it came from. We think this matters as much as the facts themselves. Children remember what they do with their own hands, and here they learn that power on Mars depends on the Sun's height and the dust, that water is recycled and never thrown away, that a call home takes minutes, and that a solar storm is something you plan for. They also learn to ask whether a thing is real and who measured it, which is the habit science depends on.

We built it with TypeScript, three.js on WebGL2, the Rapier physics engine, Vite and Vitest. The painted look builds on the open-source Oil paint renderer by @blendi. Node scripts fetch and crop the NASA and USGS data and write a source record beside every file. Playwright drives scripted playtests in a headless browser, and the site is hosted on Vercel. We used an AI code assistant (Claude) for code assistance and playtest help.

What is creative about it is that the art is the interface. There are no bars or menus in the main view, and the state of the base is read from the painting itself. The data is not a backdrop either: the real Sun runs the power, the real storm sets the countdown, and the real stars are what the telescope sees.

We designed for the age group throughout. On-screen sentences are 20 words at most, in words a seven-year-old knows, and the main view uses pictures. The mouse alone can play: click to walk, drag to look, click a machine to go to it. Shapes as well as colours tell things apart, and motion is reduced when the device asks for it. Reaching the radiation limit sends the astronaut indoors and nobody is hurt. Nothing made up is shown as real, saved data is never called live, and no NASA logos or mission badges are used.
dataRefs: NASA JPL Horizons (positions of the Sun, Earth, Phobos and Deimos from Gale Crater)
Mars MSL Gale Merged DEM 1m v3 (HiRISE terrain; NASA/JPL/University of Arizona, hosted by USGS)
Mars MSL Gale Merged Orthophoto Mosaic 25cm v3 (HiRISE imagery, hosted by USGS)
Mars MGS MOLA and MEX HRSC Blended DEM Global 200m v2 (the skyline)
NASA GISS Mars24 Sunclock: algorithm (Mars time of day)
NASA: InSight waits out dust storm (dust and solar power)
NASA: Curiosity's SAM instrument finds water in surface sample
NASA Technical Reports Server: Logistics beyond LEO (oxygen and water per astronaut)
projectRefs: HYG star database v4.1 (Hipparcos from ESA, Yale Bright Star and Gliese catalogues; CC BY-SA 4.0)
ESA Mars Express HRSC, part of the blended global elevation model above (ESA/DLR/FU Berlin)
NASA watches Mars light up during epic solar storm (NASA/JPL release, as carried by Phys.org: the 8,100 microgray dose)
Space.com: Solar storm douses Mars in radiation (Curiosity's normal daily dose)
Space.com: 98% water recovery on the Space Station
Earth.com: MOXIE has extracted oxygen from the Mars atmosphere
Oil paint renderer and figure code by @blendi (MIT and CC0)
